title: Man. Post. Cap. IV: GAR 2 formal/causal; PLAC actualis/habitualis
pass_a_gloss: GAR. 2. If we attend the matter carefully, it will appear that active privation of justice, by which namely a man loses justice and strips himself of it, is not formally the same as violation of the divine precept. And so it will indeed be true in a causal sense that violation of the divine precept is privation of justice, because namely from the violation that privation follows; in which sense pain is called a solution of the continuum, because it follows upon solution of the continuum: but in a formal sense it will not be true, namely so that in the thing itself they are one and the same and differ only in names. PLAC. But I judge that privation ought to be distinguished according to the distinction of the term or form of which it is the privation. Now justice is twofold, actual namely and habitual. The form of moral evil or of sin is usually placed in the privation of a good. Therefore privation of actual justice is formally actual sin; but privation of habitual justice is formally habitual evil or sin. Is it not so? Since therefore actual violation of the law is formally opposed to actual justice, that is, disobedience to obedience, it is necessary that actual violation of the law be formally actual privation of justice, and since habitual violation of the law or disobedience is formally opposed to habitual justice or obedience, it is necessary that it also be formally privation of habitual justice, and so habitual sin. But against this the Learned Man disputes with three reasons.
pass_b_english: Garissoles' second reply. Attend carefully and active privation of righteousness—losing it and stripping oneself of it—is not formally identical with breaking the divine precept. Causally one may say precept-breaking is privation of righteousness, because the privation follows the breach (as pain is called a dissolving of continuity because it follows that dissolving). Formally they are not one thing under two names.

Placeus. I take privation to track the form of which it is the privation. Righteousness itself is twofold: actual and habitual. Moral evil, or sin, is usually formalized as privation of a good. So privation of actual righteousness is formally actual sin, and privation of habitual righteousness is formally habitual evil or sin. Is that not so? Actual law-breaking stands formally opposite actual righteousness—disobedience opposite obedience—so actual law-breaking is formally actual privation of righteousness. Likewise habitual disobedience stands formally opposite habitual righteousness, so it too is formally privation of habitual righteousness, that is, habitual sin. Against this the learned man brings three arguments.
source_text: GAR. 2. Si rem diligenter attendimus, patebit privationem activam justitiae, qua scil. homo amittit justitiam & ea seipsum spoliat, non esse formaliter idem cum violatione praecepti divini. Itaque verum quidem erit in sensu causali violationem divini praecepti esse justitiae privationem, quia scilicet ex violatione consequitur illa privatio; quo sensu dicitur dolor esse solutio continui, quia ad solutionem continui sequitur: sed in sensu formali non erit verum, ita scilicet ut reapse unum idemque sint, nec differant, nisi nominibus. PLAC. Ego vero existimo, privationem pro distinctione termini seu formae, cujus est privatio, distingui debere. Est autem justitia duplex, actualis nempe, & habitualis. Forma mali moralis, seu peccati collocari solet in privatione boni. Justitiae igitur actualis privatio est formaliter peccatum actuale; justitiae vero habitualis privatio est formaliter malum seu peccatum habituale. Nonne? Cum ergo actualis violatio legis formaliter opponatur justitiae actuali, hoc est, inobedientia obedientiae, necesse est ut actualis violatio legis sit formaliter actualis privatio justitiae, & cum habitualis violatio legis seu inobedientia formaliter opponatur habituali justitiae seu obedientiae, necesse est ut ipsa quoque sit formaliter privatio justitiae habitualis, atque adeo peccatum habituale. Sed contra disputat Vir Doctus tribus rationibus.
